opening_summary: Thirty terms for modeling a game asset in Blender, from the parts of the window to meshes, transforms, modifiers and materials. The exact term lets you tell an AI coding agent precisely what to change.
opening_description: 30 Blender terms: window, mesh, transforms, UVs.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers often say an object's scale is its size. It is not. Scale is a multiplier left on the object, and size is the real dimensions you end up with. A pole can look right and still be a two metre cube wearing a small scale. This film goes through the Blender terms, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.
idea.replacementWords: a multiplier on the mesh's size

beats.narration: This table is the map. Thirty terms for modeling a game asset in Blender, by hand or through the Blender MCP, the Model Context Protocol link an agent uses. First, the Blender window. 3D viewport, outliner, properties editor, timeline, workspace, Object Mode, Edit Mode and collection.
The second group is mesh anatomy. Mesh, vertex, edge, face, quad, polygon count, normal and flipped normals. These terms say what a model is made of, and how it is counted.

The third group is placing and measuring. Transform, origin, pivot, apply transforms, local and global space, unit, and right-handed, plus Z up. These terms say where a model sits, how big it is, and which way is up.

The fourth group is shaping and surfacing. Modifier, mirror, subdivision surface, bevel, UV map, named for the U and V axes of an image, unwrapping, and material versus texture. These terms say how a model is built faster, and how it gets its look.

This is a drawing of the Blender window, cut into four areas. The 3D viewport, lit in red on the left, is the area where you look at the scene in three dimensions and edit it. Here a cube turns inside it. Every other area shows or changes something about what you see there. For example, to start the Blender MCP connection by hand, you press N in the 3D viewport and open the MCP for Blender tab.

The Outliner, at the top right, is a tree that lists every object and collection in the scene. Here it lists three objects in one collection, Cube, Camera and Light, and Cube is selected. Click a name and that object is selected. For example, after an agent's script builds a checkpoint post for a platformer, the Outliner lists its base, its pole, its pennant and its collision hull by name, so you can see that each part exists.

The Properties editor, below it, holds tabs of settings for whichever object is selected, such as its transform, its modifiers and its material. With the Cube selected, it shows the Cube's location, zero, zero and one metre. The Outliner lists what is in the scene, and the Properties editor shows the settings of one selected thing. For example, select the pennant of a checkpoint post, and the Properties editor shows which material it uses and lets you change it.

Five tabs sit across the top of this simplified Blender window. A Workspace is a saved arrangement of editors for one job, picked from those tabs. The tabs change which editors you see, not the scene. Here the tabs light in turn and stop on Animation, with three editors on screen. For example, to lay out the image on a crate you switch to the UV Editing workspace, and to set up its material you switch to Shading, and the crate itself never changes.

The Timeline holds the playback controls and a frame scale with keyframes marked as diamonds. Here keyframes at frames one, thirty and sixty move the red block from zero to four metres along a rail and back. The values between keys are worked out for you. A workspace decides which editors you see, and the timeline is about frames and playback. For example, a coin that bobs above a platform can be three keyframes on its height, played on the timeline.

A cube glides across the view. In Object Mode you work on whole objects. You move, rotate and scale them, and the mesh inside is not touched. Here one move carries all eight vertices together, five point nine units, and only the cube's location changes. For example, in Object Mode you lift a finished crate onto a platform, and its shape stays exactly as you built it.

Edit Mode opens the mesh itself, so you work on its vertices, edges and faces. Here one vertex, the red dot, is pulled up, and the other seven stay. The shape changes, and the object's location does not. Object Mode treats the cube as one thing, and Edit Mode treats it as eight points. For example, to give a crate a sloping lid, you enter Edit Mode and raise the vertices along one side of its top.

A Collection is a named group of objects that you can hide, show or export together. Here Props holds the post and the pennant, and Level holds the floor, the wall and the lamp. Hiding Level hides all three at once, so two of five objects stay visible. For example, keep a checkpoint post and its pennant in one collection, so you can export just that prop for Godot without the test floor around it.

A plain cube, drawn solid. A Mesh is the set of vertices, edges and faces that make a 3D shape. It is the shape's points, lines and surfaces, and it carries the model's real size. For example, a checkpoint post built for a platformer is made of separate meshes for its base, its pole and its pennant, plus a simple box mesh that Godot turns into collision.

Now each corner turns red. A Vertex is a corner point of a mesh, one position in space. Every corner of the cube is one vertex, eight in all. A vertex is a point, and an edge is a line between two points. For example, the far corner of the flat pennant on a checkpoint post is one vertex, and moving it in Edit Mode changes the pennant's shape.

Red lines now join the dots. An Edge is a line joining two vertices. Counted once each, the cube has twelve, and each one is shared by two faces. For example, the line where the top of a stair step meets its front, where the player's foot lands, is one edge of the step's mesh.

The sides are tinted now. A Face is a flat surface bounded by edges, the part that is filled in and drawn. The cube has six. For any closed shape with no holes, vertices minus edges plus faces is two. Eight minus twelve plus six is two, and a prism gives two as well. For example, an agent building a pennant once failed with the error face already exists, because it laid a back face over the same vertices as the front one.

A square splits along a diagonal into two triangles. A Quad is a face with four vertices. The GPU, the graphics processor, draws only triangles, so each quad is split in two. The cube's six quads become twelve triangles. For example, a floor tile under the player in a platformer can be modelled as one quad, and the engine draws it as two triangles.

Four bars, four tallies of the same cube. Polygon count is not one number. Blender shows six faces. The engine budgets by triangles, twelve. Blender counts eight vertices, but the GPU splits a vertex wherever its faces need different normals or UVs, so this hard-edged cube needs twenty-four. Face count is what Blender shows, and triangle count is what the engine budgets. For example, if a prop must stay under a triangle budget, ask the agent for its triangle count, not its face count.

A ring of twelve faces, each with an arrow, and light from the upper left. A Normal is the direction a surface faces, the arrow out of the face. Lighting uses it, and so does culling, which skips faces that point away from the camera. Faces turned toward the light are bright, six of twelve here. For example, a checkpoint post's pennant is a single face, so its normal points out of one side, and you check it still shows from the other.

Three arrows turn red and point inward. Flipped normals are faces whose normals point into the shape, so they face away from the light. They look dark, or are not drawn at all. Here three are flipped, and only three of twelve faces are still lit. A normal says which way a face points, and a flipped one points inward. For example, if one side of a crate shows in Godot as a black patch or a see-through hole, check for flipped normals.

A square on a grid, seen from above. Transform means three things on an object. Location is where it is, rotation is how it is turned, and scale is how much it is stretched. Here the square moves to three, one point five, turns forty-five degrees, and grows by one point six. The mesh itself is not touched. For example, placing a coin above a platform, tilting it and making it a little bigger changes only the coin's transform.

Two posts, each one point eight metres, placed at height zero. The Origin is the point an object's position and rotation are measured from. On the left the origin is in the middle, so half the post sinks into the floor, to minus zero point nine metres. On the right the origin is at the base, and the post stands on the floor. For example, the platformer's checkpoint post has its origin under the centre of its base, so it stands where it is placed.

A bar two units long, turned sixty degrees two ways. A Pivot is the point an object rotates and scales around. Turned about its middle, the tip moves a little. Turned about its end, like a hinge, it swings far, out to one, one point seven. The origin is where an object is measured from, and the pivot is what a turn happens around. For example, a door in a level should swing on a pivot at its hinge edge, not at its centre.

A table of a pole's numbers. Apply transforms bakes the object's rotation and scale into the mesh and resets them to neutral. This pole is a two metre cube scaled to zero point one, zero point one, zero point nine. After apply, the scale reads one, one, one, and the mesh is one point eight metres tall. Scale is a multiplier, and size is the real dimensions. For example, apply a pole's scale before export, so a collider built from it is not stretched.

A parent shape turns on a grid. Local and global space are two ways to give one point's position. Local coordinates are measured from the object's own origin, global ones from the scene's. As the parent turns, the red point stays at local one, zero point five, while its global position becomes four point one two, three point four three. For example, a coin riding on a moving platform keeps its local position on it, while its global position changes as the platform travels.

A player and a post, side by side. A Unit is the length one coordinate step stands for, usually a metre. In Blender, in glTF, the GL Transmission Format, and in Godot, one unit is one metre, so nothing converts. The dashed post is one point eight units beside the two point one metre player. In this made-up wrong case, take a unit as a centimetre and the post nearly vanishes. For example, a crate modelled one unit tall arrives in Godot one metre tall.

Blender's axes beside Godot's. Right-handed, plus Z up, is how Blender sets its axes. Right-handed means X cross Y gives Z, and in Blender Z points up. Godot is right-handed too, but puts plus Y up, as glTF does. The exporter's plus Y Up option moves the post's one point eight Z extent onto Godot's Y, so it stands. For example, a checkpoint post is tall along Blender's Z, and if it arrives lying on its side in Godot, the plus Y Up option was off.

A base mesh, a modifier and a result. A Modifier is a live step that changes a mesh without editing it. Here it is Subdivision Surface at level one. The base cube has eight vertices and six faces, and the result has twenty-six and twenty-four. Switch it off and the base is back. A modifier stays live, and apply bakes its result in. For example, an agent exporting a checkpoint post can be told to apply modifiers, so Godot gets the finished shape.

Now half a shape beside a dashed line. The Mirror modifier copies the mesh across an axis, so you model only one half. Here you place five vertices on the right, and the mirror across the line x equals zero makes a shape with eight. Edit one side and the other always matches. For example, model the left half of a robot enemy's head, and the Mirror modifier keeps the right half identical while you work.

One face's outline gains corners at each level. Subdivision Surface is a modifier that splits faces and smooths them, and on an all-quad mesh each level makes four times as many faces. On the cube that is six, then twenty-four, then ninety-six. Watch the triangle budget. For example, a rounded boulder for a level can start as a cube with Subdivision Surface on top, set to the lowest level that still looks smooth.

Four squares, from sharp to round. Bevel turns a sharp edge or corner into a small slanted or rounded one. A sharp edge has no width, so it cannot catch a highlight. Here the square has four vertices when sharp, then eight, twelve and sixteen as the bevel goes from one segment to three. More segments give a rounder edge and more vertices. For example, bevel the edges of a crate a little, so the light in the game catches its corners.

A cube beside a cross of six cells. A UV map is the flattened 2D layout of a mesh, used to place a texture. U and V are the two axes of the image. Each numbered face has a matching cell, where it reads the texture. A UV map is the flat layout, and a material is the whole surface recipe. For example, the UV map of a crate decides which part of a wood image lands on its lid and which on its sides.

The faces fly off the cube and lie flat. Unwrapping is cutting a mesh along seams and flattening it into a UV map. The red lines are the seams, the cuts. A cube has twelve edges, and laid out as a cross, five stay joined and seven are cut. For example, to unwrap a barrel for a level, you cut a seam down its side and around each end, so the body lies flat as one strip.

A material card beside a checker image. Material versus texture. A material is the full surface recipe, its base colour, how metallic it is and how rough. A texture is one image the material can read, here filling the base colour slot. One material can use no texture, one, or many, and these values are only illustrative. For example, the checkpoint post uses a material named PostMetal for its base and pole and FlagCloth for its pennant, and either could read a texture or none.

Look-alike pairs, side by side. The Origin is the object's own point, where its position and rotation are measured from. The Pivot is the point a turn or stretch happens around. Here the pivot is set to a corner, so the square swings about that corner.

Scale is a multiplier left on the object, here zero point five, while the mesh is still two metres. Size is the real dimensions you end up with. Scale times mesh gives what you see, one metre. Apply transforms moves that size into the mesh.
Face count is what Blender shows, six faces for the cube. Triangle count is what the engine budgets, twelve triangles, because each quad is drawn as two. Compare models by the count the budget uses.

A Material is the whole surface recipe, its colour, roughness, metal and the rest. A Texture is one image the recipe can use, a picture and nothing more. Swap the texture and the recipe stays the same.

Five vague requests to an agent driving Blender, each made exact. Make it smoother becomes, add a Subdivision Surface modifier at level two. The chart shows the faces go from six to twenty-four to ninety-six.
I only want to model half becomes, add a Mirror modifier on X and model five vertices. The shape has eight, so you place thirty-eight percent fewer.

It lies on its side in Godot becomes, export glTF with plus Y Up, so Blender's Z extent of one point eight metres lands on Godot's Y. Without it the post is zero point two metres tall. With it, one point eight.

The scale is wrong becomes, select it, then Object, Apply, Rotation and Scale. The scale goes from zero point one, zero point one, zero point nine to one, one, one. The mesh height drops from two metres to one point eight, and the size you see stays the same.

The model is too heavy becomes, look at the triangle count, then lower the subdivision level. Each level quadruples the triangles. Level three is seven hundred sixty-eight triangles, and level one is forty-eight.
This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you hand a model to the game. First, is the origin where you want to place it, such as at the base of a post, so it stands on the floor?
Second, is the scene in metres, with a unit scale of one point zero, so that one unit means one metre in Blender, in glTF and in Godot?
Third, is the transform applied, so the scale reads one, one, one? A scale left on the object is carried into anything built from its mesh, such as a collider.
Fourth, do all normals point out, so no face looks dark or goes missing? A flipped normal turns its face away from the light.
Fifth, is the triangle count within budget after the modifiers run? Each subdivision level multiplies the triangles, so count them after the modifiers, not before.
Sixth, is it unwrapped, and does each material have the name the game expects? Then say it exactly. Not fix the scale, but apply rotation and scale, then check it reads one, one, one.

recap_lines: The 3D viewport shows the scene, and the outliner lists what is in it.
Object Mode moves whole objects, and Edit Mode changes the mesh itself.
Engines budget by triangles, while Blender shows the face count.
The origin is where an object is measured from, the pivot what it turns around.
Apply transforms so the mesh carries the real size and scale reads one, one, one.
A material is the whole surface recipe, and a texture is one image it uses.

your_turn.command: Quiz me on Blender modeling terms with short game-making cases, one at a time. Use the terms Object Mode, Edit Mode, origin, pivot, apply transforms, face count, triangle count, modifier, material and texture. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me whether I was right.
checks: Check: every case is a modeling task from a game, and the answer waits.
Check: you gave the exact term and said why the look-alike does not fit.

deck_problems: Slide 6 (Quads, triangles and the polygon count), step 2: the Polygon count entry says 'Three tallies of one mesh', but the chart beside it is titled 'FOUR TALLIES OF THE SAME CUBE' and the note says 'One mesh, four numbers'.

Slide 10 (Units and the right-handed +Z up axes): the TELL THESE APART box sets 'Right-handed' against 'Y up (Godot)' as if they were opposites. Handedness and the up axis are separate properties, and Chapter 3 says Godot is right-handed too ('Godot is right-handed and Y-up'). The narration says Godot is right-handed as well.

Slide 10 step 2 prints 'extents 0.2, 1.8, 0.2' and 'extents 0.2, 0.2, 1.8' for full sizes. The course glossary defines Extents as 'The half-sizes of a bounding box', so by that definition these are sizes, and the extents would be 0.1, 0.9, 0.1. The narration says 'Z extent' only as the slide's note and slide 14 do.

Slide 13 step 2 (pair 2): Size is defined as 'The real dimensions in the mesh', but the picture shows 'size 1.00 m' worked out as 'scale × mesh = what you see' while 'the mesh is still 2 m'. By the printed definition the size in the mesh would be 2 m. The narration says 'the real dimensions you end up with' and leaves out 'in the mesh'.
Slide 9 step 1: the grey divider line in the table runs through the red 'Size you see (m)' row, so that row looks struck through.
Slide 9 step 1: the Apply transforms entry says 'Bake position, rotation and scale', but Chapter 3 and slide 14 step 4 apply Rotation & Scale only (the chapter's script passes location=False).
Slide 12 step 3: the red curve from the checker texture runs across the label '← filled by the texture', striking it through. The image slot it points to stays an empty box.

Slide 13 step 1 (pair 1): at the end of the step both turned squares overlap their own captions ('origin: the object's own point', 'pivot: set to a corner here'), so the captions are hard to read. Slide 13 step 4: the three unlabelled bars under 'colour, roughness, metal…' end with metal at about 0.8, while slide 12 step 3 shows Metallic 0.0.

Slide 4 step 2 and slide 5 steps 2 to 4: the hidden back corner of the cube is drawn as a dot on top of the front face, so a vertex seems to float in the middle of a face (most visible at slide 5 step 4).

Slide 4 step 1: the caption 'All 8 vertices moved together, 5.9 units' sits next to the note 'the mesh is untouched'. In Object Mode only the object's location changes, so 'vertices moved' can read as an edit to the mesh. The 5.9 is a screen distance (410 px over a 70 px drawing scale), not a value Blender would report.

Slide 11 step 3: the picture is one face's outline whose corners double each level (4, 8, 16), but the labels under it give the whole cube's face counts (6, 24, 96). A viewer can take '24 faces' as the count for the one drawn outline.
Slide 5 step 1: the Mesh entry and its note say 'the chapter calls it mesh data' and 'what the chapter means by mesh data'. In a standalone film there is no chapter on screen.
